claim: Mitochondria move throughout neuronal dendrites and localize to sites of energy demand.
source: Mitochondria move throughout neuronal dendrites and localize to sites of energy demand.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The prevailing view of dendritic mitochondria as highly motile organelles whose distribution is continually adjusted by neuronal activity via Ca2+-dependent arrests is based on observations in cultured neurons exposed to artificial stimuli.
source: The prevailing view of dendritic mitochondria as highly motile organelles whose distribution is continually adjusted by neuronal activity via Ca2+-dependent arrests is based on observations in cultured neurons exposed to artificial stimuli.
evidence: This statement references prior work in the field and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: During development, 30% of mitochondria are motile at any time in ganglion cell dendrites in the intact retina.
source: We find that whereas during development 30% of mitochondria are motile at any time, as dendrites mature, mitochondria all but stop moving and localize stably to synapses and branch points.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: As dendrites mature, mitochondria all but stop moving and localize stably to synapses and branch points.
source: We find that whereas during development 30% of mitochondria are motile at any time, as dendrites mature, mitochondria all but stop moving and localize stably to synapses and branch points.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Neither spontaneous nor sensory-evoked activity and Ca2+ transients alter motility of dendritic mitochondria.
source: Neither spontaneous nor sensory-evoked activity and Ca2+ transients alter motility of dendritic mitochondria; and pathological hyperactivity in a mouse model of retinal degeneration elevates rather than reduces motility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Pathological hyperactivity in a mouse model of retinal degeneration elevates rather than reduces motility of dendritic mitochondria.
source: Neither spontaneous nor sensory-evoked activity and Ca2+ transients alter motility of dendritic mitochondria; and pathological hyperactivity in a mouse model of retinal degeneration elevates rather than reduces motility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Dendritic mitochondria reach stable positions during a critical developmental period of high motility.
source: Thus, our findings indicate that dendritic mitochondria reach stable positions during a critical developmental period of high motility, and challenge current views about the role of activity in regulating mitochondrial transport in dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Mitochondria provide energy in the form of ATP and phosphocreatine.
source: Mitochondria provide energy in the form of ATP and phosphocreatine, and participate in Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondria participate in Ca2+ signaling.
source: Mitochondria provide energy in the form of ATP and phosphocreatine, and participate in Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: In neurons, mitochondrial biosynthesis occurs in the soma.
source: In neurons, mitochondrial biosynthesis occurs in the soma, but sites of energy use and Ca2+ influx are dispersed across axonal and dendritic arbors (Davis and Clayton, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davis and Clayton, 1996.

claim: Sites of energy use and Ca2+ influx are dispersed across axonal and dendritic arbors in neurons.
source: In neurons, mitochondrial biosynthesis occurs in the soma, but sites of energy use and Ca2+ influx are dispersed across axonal and dendritic arbors (Davis and Clayton, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davis and Clayton, 1996.

claim: Neuronal mitochondria are transported throughout axons and dendrites along microtubule tracks.
source: To meet these distributed demands, neuronal mitochondria are transported throughout axons and dendrites along microtubule tracks (Ehlers, 2013; Lin and Sheng, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ehlers, 2013 and Lin and Sheng, 2015.

claim: Axonal mitochondria have been examined in detail in vivo, including in peripheral and central axons.
source: A number of recent studies have explored the dynamics and function of axonal mitochondria, including detailed analyses of mitochondrial movements in peripheral and central axons in vivo (Breckwoldt et al., 2014; Misgeld et al., 2007; Plucinska et al., 2012; Takihara et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Dendritic mitochondria are less explored than axonal mitochondria.
source: By comparison, dendritic mitochondria are less explored and their dynamics have not been examined in intact neural circuits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review presented.

claim: The dynamics of dendritic mitochondria have not been examined in intact neural circuits.
source: By comparison, dendritic mitochondria are less explored and their dynamics have not been examined in intact neural circuits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review presented.

claim: Most of the energy in dendrites is consumed at synapses.
source: Most of the energy in dendrites is consumed at synapses (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Howarth et al., 2012), which are also a primary site of Ca2+ influx (Augustine et al., 2003; Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Attwell and Laughlin, 2001 and Howarth et al., 2012.

claim: Synapses are a primary site of Ca2+ influx in dendrites.
source: Most of the energy in dendrites is consumed at synapses (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Howarth et al., 2012), which are also a primary site of Ca2+ influx (Augustine et al., 2003; Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Augustine et al., 2003 and Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012.

claim: Dendritic mitochondria have been shown to localize to synapses in several systems.
source: Dendritic mitochondria have been shown to localize to synapses in several systems and appear to contribute to their formation and plasticity (Chang et al., 2006; Ishihara et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Dendritic mitochondria appear to contribute to synapse formation and plasticity.
source: Dendritic mitochondria have been shown to localize to synapses in several systems and appear to contribute to their formation and plasticity (Chang et al., 2006; Ishihara et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Increased ER complexity and Golgi outposts at dendritic branch points support protein and lipid biosynthesis, and secretory trafficking.
source: Increased ER complexity and Golgi outposts at dendritic branch points support protein and lipid biosynthesis, and secretory trafficking (Cui-Wang et al., 2012; Ehlers, 2013; Horton et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Branch points are hotspots for Ca2+ signals in some dendrites.
source: In addition, branch points are hotspots for Ca2+ signals in some dendrites (Fitzpatrick et al., 2009; Larkum et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fitzpatrick et al., 2009 and Larkum et al., 2003.

claim: Mitochondria are required for dendrites to establish normal branching patterns.
source: Mitochondria are required for dendrites to establish normal branching patterns (Fukumitsu et al., 2015; Kimura and Murakami, 2014), but whether mitochondria localize to branch points is not clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fukumitsu et al., 2015 and Kimura and Murakami, 2014.

claim: Whether mitochondria localize to branch points is not clear.
source: Mitochondria are required for dendrites to establish normal branching patterns (Fukumitsu et al., 2015; Kimura and Murakami, 2014), but whether mitochondria localize to branch points is not clear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review.

claim: When associations between mitochondria and synapses or branch points emerge during development has not been examined.
source: Moreover, when associations between mitochondria and synapses or branch points emerge during development has not been examined.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review.

claim: The prevailing view of dendritic mitochondria as being highly motile is based on observations of cultured neurons isolated from embryonic tissue.
source: Finally, the prevailing view of dendritic mitochondria as being highly motile is based on observations of cultured neurons isolated from embryonic tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review.

claim: Whether the view of dendritic mitochondria as highly motile holds true for neurons in their native environments remains unknown.
source: Whether this view holds true for neurons in their native environments, and how mitochondrial motility in dendrites changes as branching and connectivity patterns stabilize during circuit maturation remains unknown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review.

claim: How mitochondrial motility in dendrites changes as branching and connectivity patterns stabilize during circuit maturation remains unknown.
source: Whether this view holds true for neurons in their native environments, and how mitochondrial motility in dendrites changes as branching and connectivity patterns stabilize during circuit maturation remains unknown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review.

claim: Neuronal activity is thought to control the movements of dendritic mitochondria.
source: Neuronal activity is thought to control the movements of dendritic mitochondria.
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field based on prior studies.

claim: Increases in intracellular Ca2+ were shown to uncouple mitochondria from motor proteins via the Ca2+-dependent adaptor protein Miro1.
source: In particular, increases in intracellular Ca2+ were shown to uncouple mitochondria from motor proteins via the Ca2+-dependent adaptor protein Miro1 (MacAskill et al., 2009; Wang and Schwarz, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to MacAskill et al., 2009 and Wang and Schwarz, 2009.

claim: The evidence supporting a leading role for activity in dendritic mitochondrial transport was obtained from cultured neurons exposed to artificial stimuli.
source: However, the evidence supporting a leading role for activity in dendritic mitochondrial transport was obtained from cultured neurons exposed to artificial stimuli (e.g. high external K+), raising the question whether physiologically occurring activity patterns in intact circuits exert a similar influence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review.

claim: In the mature retina, photoreceptors translate changes in photon flux into changes in glutamate release.
source: In the mature retina, photoreceptors translate changes in photon flux into changes in glutamate release (Figure 1), and bipolar cells (BCs) relay this signal from the outer to the inner retina where they provide excitatory input to the dendrites of RGCs (Euler et al., 2014; Masland, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Bipolar cells relay signals from the outer to the inner retina where they provide excitatory input to the dendrites of RGCs.
source: In the mature retina, photoreceptors translate changes in photon flux into changes in glutamate release (Figure 1), and bipolar cells (BCs) relay this signal from the outer to the inner retina where they provide excitatory input to the dendrites of RGCs (Euler et al., 2014; Masland, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Euler et al., 2014 and Masland, 2001, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In mice, synapses between BCs and RGCs begin to form around postnatal day 7 (P7).
source: In mice, synapses between BCs and RGCs begin to form around postnatal day 7 (P7), and connectivity patterns reach maturity around P21 (Fisher, 1979; Johnson et al., 2003; Morgan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fisher, 1979; Johnson et al., 2003; and Morgan et al., 2008.

claim: Connectivity patterns between BCs and RGCs reach maturity around P21 in mice.
source: In mice, synapses between BCs and RGCs begin to form around postnatal day 7 (P7), and connectivity patterns reach maturity around P21 (Fisher, 1979; Johnson et al., 2003; Morgan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fisher, 1979; Johnson et al., 2003; and Morgan et al., 2008.

claim: Dendrite development leads synaptogenesis in RGCs.
source: Dendrite development leads synaptogenesis, and arborization patterns become set by P15 (Kim et al., 2010; Morgan et al., 2008; Soto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2010; Morgan et al., 2008; and Soto et al., 2012.

claim: RGC arborization patterns become set by P15 in mice.
source: Dendrite development leads synaptogenesis, and arborization patterns become set by P15 (Kim et al., 2010; Morgan et al., 2008; Soto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2010; Morgan et al., 2008; and Soto et al., 2012.

claim: During development, RGCs exhibit spontaneous waves of activity, which propagate through the early visual system and shape its synaptic organization.
source: During development, RGCs exhibit spontaneous waves of activity, which propagate through the early visual system and shape its synaptic organization (Ackman et al., 2012; Kerschensteiner, 2013; Meister et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ackman et al., 2012; Kerschensteiner, 2013; and Meister et al., 1991.

claim: Retinal waves stop around the time of eye opening (P14-15 in mice).
source: Retinal waves stop around the time of eye opening (P14-15 in mice) when sensory-evoked inputs begin to drive RGC activity (Demas et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Demas et al., 2003.

claim: Sensory-evoked inputs begin to drive RGC activity around the time of eye opening (P14-15 in mice).
source: Retinal waves stop around the time of eye opening (P14-15 in mice) when sensory-evoked inputs begin to drive RGC activity (Demas et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Demas et al., 2003.

claim: BC-RGC synaptogenesis in retinal flat mounts matches in vivo rates.
source: We have previously shown that BC-RGC synaptogenesis in retinal flat mounts matches in vivo rates (Kerschensteiner et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2011; Soto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: During development, retinal circuits in flat mount preparations generate spontaneous waves of activity with patterns similar to those observed in vivo.
source: Moreover, during development, retinal circuits in this preparation generate spontaneous waves of activity with patterns similar to those observed in vivo (Ackman et al., 2012; Demas et al., 2003); and at maturity light, responses of RGCs in retinal explants closely resemble those recorded in vivo (Farrow et al., 2013; Grimes et al., 2015; Sagdullaev and McCall, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ackman et al., 2012 and Demas et al., 2003.

claim: At maturity, light responses of RGCs in retinal explants closely resemble those recorded in vivo.
source: Moreover, during development, retinal circuits in this preparation generate spontaneous waves of activity with patterns similar to those observed in vivo (Ackman et al., 2012; Demas et al., 2003); and at maturity light, responses of RGCs in retinal explants closely resemble those recorded in vivo (Farrow et al., 2013; Grimes et al., 2015; Sagdullaev and McCall, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Farrow et al., 2013; Grimes et al., 2015; and Sagdullaev and McCall, 2005.

claim: PSD95-CFP localizes specifically to BC synapses on RGC dendrites (i.e. excitatory synapses).
source: Others and we previously showed that PSD95-CFP localizes specifically to BC synapses on RGC dendrites (i.e. excitatory synapses) (Jakobs et al., 2008; Kerschensteiner et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jakobs et al., 2008; Kerschensteiner et al., 2009; and Morgan et al., 2008.

claim: Mitochondria enter dendrites to near-mature levels before most synapses are formed.
source: We found that mitochondria enter dendrites to near-mature levels before most synapses are formed (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Mitochondria in RGC dendrites are found closer to synapses than expected by chance.
source: Similar to other systems, mitochondria in RGC dendrites are found closer to synapses than expected by chance (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The synaptic localization of mitochondria was apparent from the earliest time point examined (P9).
source: This synaptic localization of mitochondria was apparent from the earliest time point examined (P9).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: At maturity, mitochondria are enriched >15-fold at branch points in RGC dendrites.
source: In addition, at maturity, mitochondria are enriched >15-fold at branch points.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The enrichment of mitochondria at branch points emerges gradually during development.
source: Unlike their localization to synapses, the enrichment of mitochondria at branch points emerges gradually during development (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Mitochondria enter RGC dendrites during early development, associate with synapses as circuits go through the trial-and-error process of establishing precise connections, and progressively accumulate at branch points even after mature arborization patterns are established.
source: Thus, mitochondria enter RGC dendrites during early development, associate with synapses as circuits go through the trial-and-error process of establishing precise connections, and progressively accumulate at branch points even after mature arborization patterns are established.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: At P9, approximately 30% of mitochondria moved at least once per minute in RGC dendrites.
source: Indeed, similar to studies on cultured neurons, we found that at P9 approximately 30% of mitochondria moved at least once per minute (i.e. motile fraction) (Figure 3A,B and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Video 1.

claim: The motile fraction of mitochondria in RGC dendrites decreases to approximately 15% by P15.
source: However, subsequently, the motile fraction of mitochondria in RGC dendrites decreases steeply, falling to approximately 15% by P15, and at P21, we observed no mitochondrial movements in dendrites of 7 RGCs imaged in four retinas for 35 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At P21, no mitochondrial movements were observed in dendrites of 7 RGCs imaged in four retinas for 35 min.
source: However, subsequently, the motile fraction of mitochondria in RGC dendrites decreases steeply, falling to approximately 15% by P15, and at P21, we observed no mitochondrial movements in dendrites of 7 RGCs imaged in four retinas for 35 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The drastic decline in mitochondrial motility is specific to mitochondria and does not reflect a general transition in dendritic trafficking.
source: This drastic decline in motility is specific to mitochondria and does not reflect a general transition in dendritic trafficking, as SKL-GFP-labeled peroxisomes (Monosov et al., 1996) in RGC dendrites remain motile at P21 (Figure 3C,D) and beyond (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: SKL-GFP-labeled peroxisomes in RGC dendrites remain motile at P21 and beyond.
source: This drastic decline in motility is specific to mitochondria and does not reflect a general transition in dendritic trafficking, as SKL-GFP-labeled peroxisomes (Monosov et al., 1996) in RGC dendrites remain motile at P21 (Figure 3C,D) and beyond (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The movement patterns of motile mitochondria at P15 were not significantly different from those observed at P9.
source: Interestingly, the movement patterns - including duration of runs, speed during uninterrupted motion, and duration of short pauses - of motile mitochondria at P15 were not significantly different from those observed at P9 (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: As circuits mature, dendritic mitochondria undergo a cargo-specific transition from a partially motile to a stationary phase, in which they preferentially localize to synapses and branch points.
source: Thus, as circuits mature dendritic mitochondria undergo a cargo-specific transition from a partially motile to a stationary phase, in which they preferentially localize to synapses and branch points.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Biolistically labeled retinal explants generate waves of activity with similar frequency and correlation structure to those observed in unlabeled preparations and in vivo.
source: We first recorded ensembles of RGCs at P9 on multielectrode arrays (MEAs, Figure 4A), confirming that biolistically labeled explants generate waves of activity with similar frequency and correlation structure to those observed in unlabeled preparations and in vivo (Figure 4C, D) (Ackman et al., 2012; Demas et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D, and citations to Ackman et al., 2012 and Demas et al., 2003.

claim: At P9, nearby RGCs (<200 μm between cell bodies) exhibited synchronous global Ca2+ transients across their dendritic arbors.
source: At P9, nearby RGCs (<200 μm between cell bodies) exhibited synchronous global Ca2+ transients across their dendritic arbors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The frequency and correlation of Ca2+ transients in RGC dendrites was indistinguishable from that of spike bursts in MEA recordings.
source: The frequency and correlation of these transients was indistinguishable from that of spike bursts in MEA recordings (Figure 4B–D), indicating that global Ca2+ transients in RGC dendrites accompany retinal waves (Lohmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Global Ca2+ transients in RGC dendrites accompany retinal waves.
source: The frequency and correlation of these transients was indistinguishable from that of spike bursts in MEA recordings (Figure 4B–D), indicating that global Ca2+ transients in RGC dendrites accompany retinal waves (Lohmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-D and a citation to Lohmann et al., 2002.

claim: Wave-associated Ca2+ transients do not alter mitochondrial motility in RGC dendrites.
source: Simultaneous imaging of dendritic Ca2+ signals and mitochondrial movements (Figure 4E), revealed that wave-associated Ca2+ transients do not alter mitochondrial motility in RGC dendrites: neither the instantaneous motile fraction (Figure 4H and Video 2) nor the average speed of moving mitochondria (△ speed: 0.132 ± 0.067 μm/s, n = 66 mitochondria, p>0.1) change following a dendritic Ca2+ transient.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E, H and Video 2.

claim: Neither the instantaneous motile fraction nor the average speed of moving mitochondria change following a dendritic Ca2+ transient.
source: Simultaneous imaging of dendritic Ca2+ signals and mitochondrial movements (Figure 4E), revealed that wave-associated Ca2+ transients do not alter mitochondrial motility in RGC dendrites: neither the instantaneous motile fraction (Figure 4H and Video 2) nor the average speed of moving mitochondria (△ speed: 0.132 ± 0.067 μm/s, n = 66 mitochondria, p>0.1) change following a dendritic Ca2+ transient.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H and Video 2.

claim: Miro1 is readily detected in Western blots of the retina from at least P6 onwards.
source: Miro1 is readily detected in Western blots of the retina from at least P6 onwards and its expression reaches mature levels by P15 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Miro1 expression reaches mature levels by P15 in the retina.
source: Miro1 is readily detected in Western blots of the retina from at least P6 onwards and its expression reaches mature levels by P15 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Biolistic delivery of wild-type Miro1 or of a Ca2+-binding-deficient mutant (Miro1KK) does not alter the motility of dendritic mitochondria.
source: In addition, we found that biolistic delivery of wild-type Miro1 or of a Ca2+-binding-deficient mutant (Miro1KK) does not alter the motility of dendritic mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A lack of Miro1 expression or function is unlikely to account for the lack of effect of physiologic activity patterns on the movements of mitochondria in RGC dendrites.
source: Thus, a lack of Miro1 expression or function is unlikely to account for the lack of effect of physiologic activity patterns on the movements of mitochondria in RGC dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Miro1 expression and overexpression data.

claim: Elevating external K+ to 30 mM tonically increased the concentration of Ca2+ in RGC dendrites.
source: Elevating external K+ to 30 mM tonically increased the concentration of Ca2+ in RGC dendrites and, similar to observations in cultured neurons, decreased the motile fraction of mitochondria (Figure 4F, I and Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F, I and Video 3.

claim: Elevating external K+ to 30 mM decreased the motile fraction of mitochondria in RGC dendrites, similar to observations in cultured neurons.
source: Elevating external K+ to 30 mM tonically increased the concentration of Ca2+ in RGC dendrites and, similar to observations in cultured neurons, decreased the motile fraction of mitochondria (Figure 4F, I and Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F, I and Video 3.

claim: Blocking cholinergic retinal waves and the accompanying Ca2+ transients with the nicotinic antagonist DhβE did not affect mitochondrial motility in RGC dendrites.
source: By contrast, blocking cholinergic retinal waves and the accompanying Ca2+ transients with the nicotinic antagonist DhβE did not affect mitochondrial motility in RGC dendrites (Figure 4G, J and Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G, J and Video 3.

claim: A subset of RGCs (21 of 59 cells) exhibited local dendritic Ca2+ transients at a similar frequency as global signals.
source: A subset of RGCs (21 of 59 cells) exhibited local dendritic Ca2+ transients at a similar frequency as global signals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, local: 0.0102 ± 0.0055 events / s, n = 7 cells, global: 0.0141 ± 0.0022 events / s, n = 32 cells, p>0.4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Local Ca2+ transients in developing mouse RGC dendrites do not appear to alter mitochondrial motility.
source: Like global signals, local Ca2+ transients in developing mouse RGC dendrites do not appear to alter mitochondrial motility (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Physiologically occurring activity patterns and Ca2+ transients in the developing retina do not regulate mitochondrial motility in RGC dendrites, irrespective of Miro1 expression.
source: Together these results suggest that physiologically occurring activity patterns and Ca2+ transients in the developing retina do not regulate mitochondrial motility in RGC dendrites, irrespective of Miro1 expression, and that tonic elevations of Ca2+ upon application of high K+ solution may engage different mechanisms to physiological transients.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Tonic elevations of Ca2+ upon application of high K+ solution may engage different mechanisms to physiological transients.
source: Together these results suggest that physiologically occurring activity patterns and Ca2+ transients in the developing retina do not regulate mitochondrial motility in RGC dendrites, irrespective of Miro1 expression, and that tonic elevations of Ca2+ upon application of high K+ solution may engage different mechanisms to physiological transients.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Mitochondria rarely changed position even across two imaging intervals at P21 in darkness.
source: In darkness, mitochondria rarely changed position even across two imaging intervals at P21, whereas approximately half of them were displaced over the same time at P9 (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Approximately half of mitochondria were displaced over two imaging intervals at P9.
source: In darkness, mitochondria rarely changed position even across two imaging intervals at P21, whereas approximately half of them were displaced over the same time at P9 (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Light stimulation did not alter the stability of mitochondria at P21.
source: Light stimulation did not alter the stability of mitochondria at P21 and very few changed their position in the imaging intervals (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Sensory-evoked activity does not appear to regulate the motility of dendritic mitochondria in the mature retina.
source: Thus, similar to our observations for spontaneous activity in developing circuits, sensory-evoked activity does not appear to regulate the motility of dendritic mitochondria in the mature retina.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Application of a mixture of Antimycin A and Oligomycin to P9 and P21 retinas resulted in no significant changes in the motility of mitochondria in developing or mature RGC dendrites.
source: Fast (0.9 fps) and long-interval (15 min) time-lapse imaging revealed no significant changes in the motility of mitochondria in developing or mature RGC dendrites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spontaneous oscillatory hyperactivity of RGCs is a common feature of retinal degenerations and originates in presynaptic circuits.
source: Spontaneous oscillatory hyperactivity of RGCs is a common feature of retinal degenerations and originates in presynaptic circuits (Borowska et al., 2011; Margolis et al., 2008; Soto and Kerschensteiner, 2015; Soto et al., 2012; Stasheff, 2008; Yee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In Crx-/- mice, a model of Leber congenital amaurosis, retinal waves are preserved.
source: In Crx-/- mice, a model of Leber congenital amaurosis, retinal waves are preserved.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Crx-/- mouse model.

claim: From P15 on, RGCs in Crx-/- mice exhibit rhythmic hyperactivity as a result of enhanced input from BCs.
source: But, from P15 on RGCs exhibit rhythmic hyperactivity as a result of enhanced input from BCs (Soto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Soto et al., 2012.

claim: Elevated activity in Crx-/- mice prolongs and enhances BC-RGC synaptogenesis.
source: We previously showed that this elevated activity prolongs and enhances BC-RGC synaptogenesis (Soto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Dendritic mitochondria in Crx-/- retinas remained motile at P21, at a level intermediate to those at P9 and P15 in wild-type mice.
source: We found that dendritic mitochondria in Crx-/- retinas remained motile at P21, at a level intermediate to those at P9 and P15 in wild-type mice (Figure 6D,E and Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D, E and Video 4.

claim: The movement patterns of motile mitochondria at P21 in Crx-/- mice except for slightly longer pauses were indistinguishable from those in wild-type at P9 and P15.
source: Moreover, the movement patterns of motile mitochondria at P21 in Crx-/- mice except for slightly longer pauses were indistinguishable from those in wild-type at P9 and P15 (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: Mutations that alter the fission-fusion balance and transport of mitochondria cause neurodegenerative diseases.
source: The importance of mitochondrial dynamics and distribution to neuronal function is highlighted by the fact that mutations that alter the fission-fusion balance and transport of mitochondria cause neurodegenerative diseases (Chan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chan, 2006.

claim: RGCs degenerate in autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA), the most common hereditary optic neuropathy.
source: Among the neurons affected by such diseases are RGCs, which degenerate in autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA), the most common hereditary optic neuropathy (Olichon et al., 2006; Yu-Wai-Man et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Olichon et al., 2006 and Yu-Wai-Man et al., 2011.

claim: A majority of ADOA patients harbors mutations in the OPA1 gene, which encodes a GTPase involved in mitochondrial fusion.
source: A majority of ADOA patients harbors mutations in the OPA1 gene, which encodes a GTPase involved in mitochondrial fusion (Olichon et al., 2006; Yu-Wai-Man et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Olichon et al., 2006 and Yu-Wai-Man et al., 2011.

claim: Changes in fission-fusion balance alter the transport and distribution of mitochondria in neurons.
source: Changes in fission-fusion balance alter the transport and distribution of mitochondria in neurons (Chan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chan, 2006.

claim: During development, mitochondria enter RGC dendrites to near-mature levels before branching patterns are established.
source: We find that during development mitochondria enter RGC dendrites to near-mature levels before branching patterns are established (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Similar observations of mitochondria entering dendrites to near-mature levels before branching patterns are established were recently made for dendrites of cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: Similar observations were recently made for dendrites of cerebellar Purkinje cells (Fukumitsu et al., 2015), and together with experiments that block export of mitochondria into dendrites support the notion that local mitochondria are required for the formation and/or maintenance of dendritic branches (Fukumitsu et al., 2015; Ishihara et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fukumitsu et al., 2015.

claim: Local mitochondria are required for the formation and/or maintenance of dendritic branches.
source: Similar observations were recently made for dendrites of cerebellar Purkinje cells (Fukumitsu et al., 2015), and together with experiments that block export of mitochondria into dendrites support the notion that local mitochondria are required for the formation and/or maintenance of dendritic branches (Fukumitsu et al., 2015; Ishihara et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fukumitsu et al., 2015 and Ishihara et al., 2009.

claim: During development, dendritic mitochondria gradually become enriched (>15-fold) near branch points.
source: We find that during development, dendritic mitochondria gradually become enriched (>15-fold) near branch points (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mitochondria near branch points likely provide energy for lipid and protein biosynthesis, and secretory trafficking in the complex ER structures and Golgi outposts found at branch points.
source: These mitochondria likely provide energy for lipid and protein biosynthesis, and secretory trafficking in the complex ER structures and Golgi outposts found at branch points (Cui-Wang et al., 2012; Horton et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to Cui-Wang et al., 2012; Horton et al., 2005; and Ye et al., 2007.

claim: ER structures and Golgi outposts at branch points are required for the formation and maintenance of dendritic branches.
source: Consistent with this idea, ER structures and Golgi outposts at branch points are required for the formation and maintenance of dendritic branches (Cui-Wang et al., 2012; Horton et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2007), and the branching phenotypes of neurons lacking dendritic mitochondria can be rescued by exogenous supply of ATP-phosphocreatine (Fukumitsu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cui-Wang et al., 2012; Horton et al., 2005; and Ye et al., 2007.

claim: The branching phenotypes of neurons lacking dendritic mitochondria can be rescued by exogenous supply of ATP-phosphocreatine.
source: Consistent with this idea, ER structures and Golgi outposts at branch points are required for the formation and maintenance of dendritic branches (Cui-Wang et al., 2012; Horton et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2007), and the branching phenotypes of neurons lacking dendritic mitochondria can be rescued by exogenous supply of ATP-phosphocreatine (Fukumitsu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fukumitsu et al., 2015 and Li et al., 2004.

claim: Mitochondria in RGC dendrites localize to excitatory synapses.
source: Mitochondria in RGC dendrites localize to excitatory synapses (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Similar observations of mitochondria localizing to synapses have been made on cultured neurons, although the extent of co-localization varied between studies.
source: Similar observations have been made on cultured neurons, although the extent of co-localization varied between studies (Chang et al., 2006; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2006 and Li et al., 2004.

claim: Experiments in cultured hippocampal neurons suggested that enhancing the dendritic mitochondria content is sufficient to increase the number of synapses.
source: Experiments in cultured hippocampal neurons suggested that enhancing the dendritic mitochondria content is sufficient to increase the number of synapses (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2004.

claim: It seems unlikely that mitochondria limit the rate of synaptogenesis during development of the RGC circuit, as mitochondrial density in RGCs dendrites reaches near-mature levels before most synapses are formed.
source: As mitochondrial density in RGCs dendrites reaches near-mature levels before most synapses are formed, it seems unlikely that mitochondria limit the rate of synaptogenesis during development of this circuit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Mitochondrial transport in RGC dendrites is well described by a state diagram in which mitochondria exist in a motile or a stationary state.
source: Mitochondrial transport in RGC dendrites is well described by a state diagram recently applied to axonal transport, in which mitochondria exist in a motile or a stationary state (Obashi and Okabe, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Obashi and Okabe, 2013.

claim: Motile mitochondria alternate between short runs and short pauses.
source: Motile mitochondria alternate between short runs and short pauses (Figure 3) and frequently switch the direction of their movements (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Stationary mitochondria remain in place for long periods of time.
source: By contrast, stationary mitochondria remain in place for long periods of time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Transitions between motile and stationary state are rare for mitochondria.
source: Unlike transitions between runs and pauses in the motile state, transitions between motile and stationary state are rare (Obashi and Okabe, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Obashi and Okabe, 2013.

claim: As circuits mature, dendritic mitochondria undergo a nearly complete shift to the stationary state.
source: Our results show that as circuits mature, dendritic mitochondria undergo a nearly complete shift to the stationary state.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Rare displacements of mitochondria at P21 may be associated with mitochondrial fission or support mitochondrial fusion or mitophagy.
source: These rare displacements may be associated with mitochondrial fission or support mitochondrial fusion or mitophagy (Chen and Chan, 2009; Maday and Holzbaur, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to Chen and Chan, 2009 and Maday and Holzbaur, 2014.

claim: Disruption of mitochondrial fusion in a mouse model of ADOA (Opa1+/- mice) results in shortened mitochondria, which accumulate in proximal RGC dendrites.
source: Disruption of mitochondrial fusion in a mouse model of ADOA (Opa1+/- mice) results in shortened mitochondria, which accumulate in proximal RGC dendrites (Williams et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Williams et al., 2012.

claim: As Opa1+/- mice age (>1 yr), the number of excitatory synapses and branches of RGC dendrites declines.
source: As Opa1+/- mice age (>1 yr), the number of excitatory synapses and branches of RGC dendrites declines, highlighting the importance of mitochondrial fusion for dendritic and synaptic integrity (Williams et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Williams et al., 2010 and Williams et al., 2012.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion is important for dendritic and synaptic integrity.
source: As Opa1+/- mice age (>1 yr), the number of excitatory synapses and branches of RGC dendrites declines, highlighting the importance of mitochondrial fusion for dendritic and synaptic integrity (Williams et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Williams et al., 2010 and Williams et al., 2012.

claim: In isolated cortical neurons, a modest decline in mitochondrial motility was observed with increasing time in culture.
source: In isolated cortical neurons, a modest decline in mitochondrial motility was observed with increasing time in culture (Chang and Reynolds, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chang and Reynolds, 2006.

claim: In the intact retina, there is a drastic developmental shift (motile to stationary) in dendritic mitochondria.
source: In the intact retina, we discover a drastic developmental shift (motile to stationary) in dendritic mitochondria.
evidence: This is a summary of the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The developmental shift from motile to stationary is cargo-specific, as peroxisomes keep moving in dendrites of mature RGCs.
source: Importantly, this shift is cargo-specific, as peroxisomes keep moving in dendrites of mature RGCs (Figure 3), and compartment-specific, as mitochondria remain motile in RGC axons (data not shown) (Takihara et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The developmental shift from motile to stationary is compartment-specific, as mitochondria remain motile in RGC axons.
source: Importantly, this shift is cargo-specific, as peroxisomes keep moving in dendrites of mature RGCs (Figure 3), and compartment-specific, as mitochondria remain motile in RGC axons (data not shown) (Takihara et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished data and a citation to Takihara et al., 2015.

claim: Mitochondria form stable associations with synapses and branch points in RGC dendrites.
source: Together with results on dendritic localization (Figure 2), these observations reveal that mitochondria form stable associations with synapses and branch points in RGC dendrites, and suggest that the prevailing view of mitochondria as highly motile organelles applies to developing but not to mature dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The prevailing view of mitochondria as highly motile organelles applies to developing but not to mature dendrites.
source: Together with results on dendritic localization (Figure 2), these observations reveal that mitochondria form stable associations with synapses and branch points in RGC dendrites, and suggest that the prevailing view of mitochondria as highly motile organelles applies to developing but not to mature dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Neither patterned spontaneous activity during development nor sensory-evoked activity at maturity regulate the motility of mitochondria in RGC dendrites.
source: Using simultaneous two-photon imaging of Ca2+ and mitochondria in the intact retina, we find that neither patterned spontaneous activity during development (Figure 4) nor sensory-evoked activity at maturity (Figure 5) regulate the motility of mitochondria in RGC dendrites.
evidence: This is a summary of the data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Results on the lack of effect of physiologic activity on mitochondrial motility are in contrast to studies of cultured neurons, which suggest that neuronal activity controls motility of dendritic mitochondria via the adaptor protein Miro1.
source: These results are in contrast to studies of cultured neurons, which suggest that neuronal activity controls motility of dendritic mitochondria via the adaptor protein Miro1 (Li et al., 2004; MacAskill et al., 2009; Rintoul et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: Differences between activity patterns physiologically occurring in intact circuits and artificial stimuli used to elicit effects on mitochondrial motility in culture may be a contributing factor to the discrepant results on the influence of activity.
source: Thus, it seems unlikely that differences in Miro1 expression or function account for the discrepant results on the influence of activity. Instead, we suggest that differences between activity patterns physiologically occurring in intact circuits and artificial stimuli used to elicit effects on mitochondrial motility in culture may be a contributing factor.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the data.

claim: Extended synaptogenesis in Crx-/- mice is matched by an increase in mitochondrial motility at P21.
source: Here, we find that extended synaptogenesis is matched by an increase in mitochondrial motility at P21 in Crx-/- mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The parallel decline in synapse turnover and mitochondrial motility across normal development suggests that the two processes are linked.
source: Together with the parallel decline in synapse turnover and mitochondrial motility across normal development (Figure 3) (Kerschensteiner et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2008), this suggests that the two processes are linked.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figure 3 and citations to Kerschensteiner et al., 2009 and Morgan et al., 2008.
